Angels in America. Tony Kushner's two-part play, subtitled "A Gay Fantasia on National Themes," premiered between 1991 and 1993. It interweaves the personal collapse of four New Yorkers devastated by HIV and AIDS with a larger vision of American identity and redemption. The work combines kitchen-sink realism with apocalyptic fantasy, exploring grief, faith, and the possibility of change.

Millennium Approaches premiered in 1991, followed by Perestroika in 1993. The play won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1993 and became the most celebrated American play of its era. The protagonist Prior Walter is a gay man dying of AIDS. He is visited by an Angel, a biblical messenger announcing revelation and demanding that Prior stop the dying. Prior refuses. Roy Cohn, the real-life disgraced lawyer and closeted homosexual, is a central character. His death and moral reckoning serve as an indictment of power, hypocrisy, and complicity.

The play explicitly addresses the Reagan administration's negligence during the AIDS crisis, transforming personal tragedy into political critique. Hannah Pitt is the mother of a closeted Mormon lawyer. She gradually becomes an unlikely ally, and the play suggests that reconciliation is possible even across deep ideological divides. The final image is transcendent. Prior, now a survivor, addresses the audience with a vision of hope and reconstruction. He speaks of the great work that begins.

Tony Kushner's epic meditation explores American history, sexuality, and redemption. The play marks a turning point in cultural representation and public reckoning during the HIV AIDS crisis. Both Angels in America and Death of a Salesman explore the individual crushed by larger historical and economic forces, though Angels moves toward transcendence. A Raisin in the Sun features an earlier American play about marginalized community persisting despite systemic oppression. And Long Day's Journey Into Night is a family tragedy; Angels expands the form to include political and metaphysical dimensions.
